extracted.intended_audience: researchers, journal editors, science communicators, and general readers interested in academic publishing policy
extracted.subtask_description: Describes the Ingelfinger rule: a journal editorial policy refusing to publish findings that have been published elsewhere, its rationale, effects, and modern exceptions (notably treatment of preprints).

rubrics_metrics.name: No prior publication (Ingelfinger rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: "NEJM would not publish findings that had been published elsewhere."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Originally articulated in the 1969 editorial "Definition of 'Sole Contribution'" (written by Ingelfinger but published anonymously). Meant as an explicit editorial policy that journals decline to publish material that has already appeared elsewhere; the formulation has been adopted by several other scientific journals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freshness / non-duplication of journal content
rubrics_metrics.description: The rule historically helped to ensure that the journal's content is fresh and does not duplicate content previously reported elsewhere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Serves as an editorial standard for originality in published journal content; intended to avoid repetition of previously reported findings in the journal's pages and to protect the value of the journal's published material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protect the scientific embargo system
rubrics_metrics.description: The Ingelfinger rule seeks to protect the scientific embargo system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: By refusing prior-publication, journals aim to maintain control over timing of public dissemination (embargoes). The policy is tied to practices around coordinated media release and is linked to 'news embargo' norms in science communication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevent duplicate publications (ethical/metric concern)
rubrics_metrics.description: The rule has been seen as aiming to prevent authors from performing duplicate publications which would unduly inflate their publication record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Functions as a safeguard against gaming of publication counts and against redundant literature; cited literature examines prevalence and impact of duplicate publications across fields.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discourage pre-publicity / talking to media before peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: In defense of the policy, the journal said the practice discouraged scientists from talking to the media before their work was peer reviewed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This operationalizes the policy as a control on pre-publicity: authors are discouraged from publicizing results via media channels prior to peer review, to preserve review integrity and embargo practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protect journals' commercial/revenue interests (stated motive)
rubrics_metrics.description: It has also been stated that the real reason for the Ingelfinger rule is to protect the journals' revenue stream.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledges a commercial/motivational dimension to the policy: withholding prior-publication can preserve a journal's exclusivity and thereby its market value. This explanation is discussed alongside other rationales in critiques of the rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preprint / modern-exception: loosened application for preprints
rubrics_metrics.description: With the increase in popularity of preprint servers such as arXiv, bioRxiv, and HAL many journals have loosened their requirements concerning the Ingelfinger rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reflects contemporary adaptation: some journals no longer consider posting to preprint servers as 'prior publication' and therefore accept submissions that have been shared as preprints; guidance varies by journal and is catalogued in resources like lists of journals by preprint policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of applicability (originally NEJM; later adoption by others)
rubrics_metrics.description: Though originally meant only for NEJM, the guideline was subsequently adopted by several other scientific journals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indicates that the rule began as a journal-specific editorial policy but became influential across academic publishing; applicability and enforcement differ among journals and over time.
